description.sr_latin: Kako da reagovaš kao pravi Srbin — iznenađenje, frustracija, oduševljenje.
description.en: How to react like a real Serb — surprise, frustration, excitement, and everything in between.

phrases.context: Your go-to reaction for anything surprising. Used constantly in Serbian conversation.
phrases.notes: Can be genuine surprise or sarcastic, depending on tone. Very versatile.

phrases.en: Come on! / No way! / Get out!
phrases.context: Disbelief, dismissal, or 'you can't be serious.' One of the most Serbian expressions.
phrases.notes: 'Ma' adds emphasis/dismissal. 'Daj' = give. Together it's pure disbelief.

phrases.context: Stronger disbelief or flat-out refusal. Also used to express that something is impossible.
phrases.notes: 'Nema' = there is no. 'Šanse' = chance (genitive).

phrases.context: Similar to 'stvarno' but with more weight. You're genuinely asking if they're serious.
phrases.notes: 'Ozbiljan' = serious. This is the adverb form used as a question.

phrases.context: Your friend says they got the job — what do you fire back?
phrases.notes: Borrowed from English/German. Pronounced 'SOO-per' with Serbian accent.

phrases.context: Your plan comes together perfectly — react with a word stronger than 'super'.
phrases.notes: From 'odličan' = excellent. The most positive grade in Serbian schools is 'odličan' (5).

phrases.context: Your friend nailed a hard exam — tip your hat to them.
phrases.notes: Literally 'every honor.' Used to show respect and admiration. No direct English equivalent.

phrases.context: A friend shows you a clip of their weekend — react like it's awesome.
phrases.notes: Used as a standalone exclamation. Can also mean 'extra good' as an adjective.

phrases.context: Your friend tells you their flight got cancelled again — react to the bad news.
phrases.notes: Literally 'horror.' Very commonly used as a standalone reaction.

phrases.context: The Serbian 'oh no.' Used for pain, surprise, exasperation — extremely versatile.
phrases.notes: One of the most common Serbian exclamations. Pronunciation can change the meaning — short and sharp for pain, drawn out for exasperation.

phrases.context: The bus is five minutes late again — react with maximum dramatic flair.
phrases.notes: Often used with playful exaggeration. Your bus is 5 minutes late? Katastrofa.

phrases.context: When something's not worth discussing or you're frustrated explaining it.
phrases.notes: 'Pustiti' = to let go / to leave. 'Ma pusti' = dismissive 'forget about it.'

phrases.context: Your all-purpose exclamation for surprise, shock, or exasperation — used by everyone, religious or not.
phrases.notes: 'Bože' is the vocative of 'Bog' (God). Used by everyone regardless of religiosity.

phrases.context: Exasperation or overwhelm. 'Joj' adds emotional weight.
phrases.notes: 'Joj' is a uniquely Serbian exclamation — something between 'oh' and 'ugh.'

phrases.context: Emphasizing that you're telling the truth. 'I'm dead serious.'
phrases.notes: Literally 'by my God.' Used for emphasis, not literally religious.

phrases.context: The most common casual 'okay' in Serbian. Used to confirm plans, agree to something.
phrases.notes: Literally means 'it holds/applies.' Far more natural than 'okej' in most contexts.

phrases.context: Your friend lays out a plan and asks what you think — tell them you're on board.
phrases.notes: 'Slagati se' = to agree. Reflexive verb.

phrases.context: Someone asks if you're coming to the party — answer like it's totally obvious.
phrases.notes: Can be genuine or slightly sarcastic depending on delivery.

phrases.context: Your friend says out loud the exact thing you were thinking — snap back in agreement.
phrases.notes: 'Baš' = exactly/truly. 'Tako' = so/like that.

phrases.en: It doesn't matter. / No worries. / Never mind.
phrases.context: Dismissing something — either reassuring someone or brushing something off.
phrases.notes: Literally 'there's no connection.' One of the most useful Serbian phrases. Can mean 'it's okay' or 'it's not related.'

phrases.context: Strong disagreement or dismissal. 'That's ridiculous.'
phrases.notes: Literally 'what kind!' Used to reject an idea or suggestion.

phrases.context: Downplaying something. When someone thanks you or makes a big deal of something small.
phrases.notes: 'Ništa' = nothing. Very casual dismissal.

phrases.context: Impatience, frustration, or urging someone. 'Bre' is the most Serbian word ever.
phrases.notes: 'Bre' is an untranslatable Serbian particle. It adds emphasis, frustration, or camaraderie. Use it and you'll sound instantly more Serbian.

phrases.en: It's annoying me. / It's bugging me.
phrases.context: Someone keeps repeating the same complaint — say it's really getting on your nerves.
phrases.notes: 'Smarati' = to bore/annoy. Very casual/slangy.

phrases.context: Expressing boredom. Also used as a reaction to a boring story or situation.
phrases.notes: Literally 'it is boring to me.' Dative construction — the boredom happens TO you.

phrases.context: The kids won't stop bickering — snap that it has to stop now.
phrases.notes: 'Dosta' = enough. 'Više' = more/already. Together: 'enough already!'

phrases.context: When you're unsure or buying time. 'Pa' is the ultimate Serbian filler word.
phrases.notes: 'Pa' = well/so. Serbians start half their sentences with 'pa.' It's the thinking word.

phrases.context: Casual 'I have no idea.' Very natural filler.
phrases.notes: Literally 'well, what do I know.' Feels more natural than a direct 'ne znam.'

phrases.context: Enthusiastic or slightly sarcastic agreement. Context and tone determine meaning.
phrases.notes: Literally 'how not to!' Can be genuine enthusiasm or dripping sarcasm.

phrases.context: Sympathizing with someone's bad luck or difficult situation.
phrases.notes: 'Jadan' = poor/pitiful. 'Jadna' for a woman.

phrases.context: Your friend says their car got broken into — react with sympathy.
phrases.notes: 'Grozno' = terrible/awful. Strong negative reaction.

phrases.context: When someone tells you bad news. Not an apology — it's sympathy.
phrases.notes: Literally 'it is grievous to me.' Different from 'izvini' which is an actual apology.

phrases.context: You taste a friend's cooking and it's actually great — give understated Balkan praise.
phrases.notes: Serbs often express positivity through understatement. 'Nije loše' can be high praise.

phrases.context: You bite into the food a friend made and it's great — tell them sincerely.
phrases.notes: 'Baš' intensifies whatever follows. 'Dobro' = good.

phrases.context: You just saw an unbelievable goal at the match — shout how wild that was.
phrases.notes: Literally 'madness.' Used positively like English 'insane!' or 'crazy good!'

phrases.context: A friend plays you a track they love — tell them it's absolutely top.
phrases.notes: Literally 'peak/top.' Very casual, mostly younger generation.
